headline: A drawing test may help spot Parkinson's

sources.title: The Way You Draw Can Reveal Parkinson's Disease With Up to 99% Accuracy, Study Reveals (ScienceAlert)
Investigadores desarrollan un sistema que identifica señales de Parkinson a partir de ejercicios de escritura (Infobae)
Caneta inteligente e IA detectam Parkinson com 98% de precisão (Jornal Impresso Brasil / Gazeta Brasil)

chunks.text: Researchers in India say they have {{come up with}} a drawing test that can {{pick up}} signs of Parkinson's disease. It was published in the journal Discover Computing and reported on August 29, 2026. Parkinson's is a [[nerve disease]] that affects movement, and doctors often make a [[diagnosis]] only after clear [[symptoms]] {{show up}}. Handwriting changes can appear earlier, but they are often too [[subtle]] to see with the [[naked eye]].

verbs.correct: To think of a new idea or method
verbs.wrong: To face a problem while doing research
verbs.why: Students come up with excuses for late homework, and cooks come up with new recipes from leftovers. Researchers in India came up with a drawing test that looks for signs of Parkinson's disease.

verbs.correct: To notice something hard to see
verbs.why: A careful reader picks up a tiny spelling mistake on a menu, and a good teacher picks up the small signs that a student is lost. The drawing test can pick up signs of Parkinson's that are too subtle to see with the naked eye.
A stain shows up after a shirt dries, and roof problems show up in winter. Doctors often make a Parkinson's diagnosis only after clear symptoms show up, but handwriting changes can appear earlier.

chunks.text: Participants [[trace]] two patterns with a smart pen: a spiral and a meander, a [[zigzag]] line with sharp corners. The pen records the drawing plus [[pressure]], [[tilt]], and acceleration. The team {{broke the analysis down}} into two parts: computer models studied the images, and a separate model studied the pen's [[motion]] data. An algorithm then {{put the two results together}} to {{tell the two groups apart}}, people with Parkinson's and healthy people, using only their drawings.

verbs.correct: To divide something into smaller parts
verbs.why: A teacher can break a long word down into syllables, and a manager can break a big project down into weekly tasks. The team broke the analysis down into two parts: one model for the images and another for the pen motion data.

verbs.correct: To combine parts into one thing
verbs.wrong: To suggest an idea for discussion
verbs.why: A child can put a puzzle together, and a coach can put together a team from new players. An algorithm put the two results together into one final answer for each drawing.

verbs.correct: To see the difference between two groups
verbs.wrong: To sort the results by patient age
verbs.why: It is hard to tell twins apart, and some people cannot tell a real photo apart from a fake one. The goal was to tell people with Parkinson's apart from healthy people using only their drawings.

chunks.text: The study was {{carried out}} with 66 participants: 31 with Parkinson's and 35 healthy people, a [[control group]] from an earlier study in Brazil. The system reached 98.95 percent [[accuracy]] on meander drawings and 97.74 percent on spirals. But a small study does not {{rule out}} mistakes in real life. The researchers called it a [[proof of concept]], not a [[clinically validated]] tool, and said it cannot {{stand in for}} a [[neurological evaluation]]. The results still need to {{hold up}} in larger, more [[diverse]] groups.

verbs.correct: To do a piece of work or research
verbs.wrong: To continue for a longer time
verbs.why: A hospital carries out a survey of its patients, and a mechanic carries out a full check of a car. The study was carried out with 66 participants: 31 with Parkinson's and 35 healthy people.

verbs.correct: To say that something is not possible
verbs.why: A doctor can rule out a broken bone after an X-ray, and a weather report cannot rule out rain. A strong result in a small study does not rule out mistakes in real life, the researchers warned.

verbs.correct: To take the place of a person or thing
verbs.wrong: To defend a person or an idea in public
verbs.why: A nurse can stand in for a doctor at a meeting, and a substitute teacher stands in for a sick one. The researchers said the drawing test cannot stand in for a neurological evaluation by a doctor.

verbs.correct: To stay true after more testing
verbs.why: A guess about the weather may not hold up once the forecast comes in, and an excuse that sounds fine at first often does not hold up when parents check with the school. The results still need to hold up in larger and more diverse groups of people.

chunks.text: Still, the researchers are hopeful. If the results are {{backed up}} by further studies, a simple drawing task could support [[non-invasive]], low-cost [[screening]] that people could do [[remotely]], far from a hospital. The team plans to {{follow up}} with larger trials before anything can be {{rolled out}} in clinics. For now, the smart pen is a research tool, not a way to {{find out}} whether you have Parkinson's.

verbs.wrong: To drop a claim after a challenge
verbs.why: A lawyer backs up a claim with documents, and a scientist backs up a theory with data. If the results are backed up by further studies, a simple drawing task could support cheap, non-invasive screening.

verbs.correct: To do more work after a first result
verbs.wrong: To publish results in a journal
verbs.why: A clinic follows up a checkup with a phone call, and a reporter follows up a tip with more questions. The team plans to follow up with larger trials before the test goes anywhere near a clinic.

verbs.wrong: To reduce or cancel a plan
verbs.why: A city rolls out a new bus app, and a phone company rolls out an update to every customer. Nothing can be rolled out in clinics until larger trials are finished.

verbs.correct: To learn or discover a fact
verbs.wrong: To ask a doctor for a test
verbs.why: You can find out a store's hours online, and a student finds out her grade after the exam. For now the smart pen is a research tool, not a way to find out whether you have Parkinson's.

mainIdea.s: Researchers in India built a smart pen test that uses computer models to spot Parkinson's signs in drawings. They call it a proof of concept that still needs larger studies.
mainIdea.why: A smart pen records the drawings and the motion data, two computer models study them, and the researchers themselves say the results need to hold up in larger, more diverse groups.

mainIdea.s: A smart pen drawing test has been approved as a reliable way to diagnose Parkinson's disease. Clinics can now use it instead of a full neurological evaluation by a doctor.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the researchers called the test a proof of concept, not a clinically validated tool, and it cannot stand in for a doctor's evaluation.

mainIdea.s: A university in India has developed a wearable wrist sensor that tracks tremors in Parkinson's patients at home. Doctors use the data to adjust medication between hospital visits.
mainIdea.why: The test uses a smart pen and drawings, not a wrist sensor, and there is nothing about adjusting medication.

tf.s: The spiral drawings gave the most accurate results.
tf.why: The meander drawings did slightly better, at 98.95 percent accuracy against 97.74 for the spirals.

tf.s: The study was carried out with just 66 participants.
tf.why: There were 31 people with Parkinson's and 35 healthy people, whose data came from an earlier study in Brazil.

tf.s: The researchers say the test can replace a doctor's evaluation.
tf.why: They said the opposite. It is a proof of concept and cannot stand in for a neurological evaluation.

tf.s: Separate computer models studied the images and the pen motion data.
tf.why: The team broke the analysis down into two parts, and an algorithm then put the two results together into one answer.

tf.s: The team plans to roll out the test in clinics before larger trials.
tf.why: Larger trials come first. Only after that could anything be rolled out in clinics.

tf.s: Doctors often make a diagnosis only after clear symptoms show up.
tf.why: Handwriting changes can appear earlier, but they are often too subtle to see with the naked eye.
